This vignette covers the package-native route for:

- checking whether a design is connected enough for a common scale
- exporting anchor candidates from an existing fit
- screening differential facet functioning (DFF)
- deciding whether subgroup contrasts are linked and available for screening

For a broader workflow guide, see `vignette("mfrmr-workflow", package = "mfrmr")`.
For the shorter help-page map, see
`help("mfrmr_linking_and_dff", package = "mfrmr")`.

## First example: reuse selected criterion locations

An **anchor** is a parameter value held fixed during estimation. A shared
Person, rater or task is an observed link; sharing an identity does not require
fixing its value. For example, a direct Rater anchor at 0.35 logits holds that
rater's location at 0.35, whereas a group anchor at 0.20 for two raters fixes
their sum at 0.40 and lets their individual values differ.

Start by loading the packaged synthetic teaching ratings. Each row is one
Person's score from one Rater on one Criterion, on a 1--4 rubric. We split the
48 Persons into two teaching cohorts with the same four raters and four
criteria. This illustrates reuse of known identities; it is not empirical
evidence that a real rater or criterion stays invariant over time.

```{r anchor-data}
library(mfrmr)
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
head(ratings[, c("Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Score")])
people <- unique(ratings$Person)
baseline_data <- ratings[ratings$Person %in% people[1:24], , drop = FALSE]
new_data <- ratings[ratings$Person %in% people[25:48], , drop = FALSE]
```

Fit the reference and select its Criterion locations. `make_anchor_table()`
requires a numerically eligible source, but does not establish substantive
invariance. If it refuses a source, inspect that model's diagnostics; exporting
with `readiness_policy = "review"` is for inspection, not for bypassing the
requirement in a new calibration.

```{r anchor-reference}
baseline <- fit_mfrm(
  baseline_data, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  method = "MML", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve"
)
anchors <- make_anchor_table(baseline, facets = "Criterion")
anchors
```

The columns name the facet, its exact level ID, and its fixed location in
internal logit coordinates. They do not contain thresholds, slopes or source
standard errors. Values transformed for display with `Umean`/`Uscale` must not
be copied into this table as though they were internal logits. The default
`digits = NULL` preserves fitted values for reuse. Rounding each row can break
a whole-facet zero sum, so round a display copy rather than the anchor input.

Review the intended constraints against the **receiving** data before fitting.
Unknown IDs, duplicate rows and incompatible targets need resolution; keeping
the last duplicate row mechanically does not decide which value is justified.

```{r anchor-review}
anchor_review <- review_mfrm_anchors(
  new_data, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score", anchors = anchors,
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve"
)
anchor_review$issue_counts
anchor_review$anchors
anchor_review$recommendations
```

The recommendation about five anchors is a configurable count screen, not a
universal minimum or proof that a design is linked. `FreeLevels` counts levels
outside direct/group constraints, not independent parameters: group members
can vary subject to their mean, while centering removes a degree of freedom.

Now fit the new cohort. This example fixes **all four** Criterion locations,
so that facet has no unanchored remainder. Rater locations and category
thresholds are estimated again. The same rubric is specified explicitly in
both fits.

```{r anchor-new-cohort}
linked <- anchor_to_baseline(
  new_data, baseline, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  anchor_facets = "Criterion", anchor_policy = "error",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve"
)
summary(linked)
linked$fit$facets$others
linked$drift[, c("Facet", "Level", "Baseline", "New", "Drift")]
```

Read `linked$fit$facets$others` for the fitted facet locations. `linked$drift`
compares only retained **fixed non-Person anchors**: its zero differences are
expected by construction and do not test stability. For independent screening,
fit waves separately and use `detect_anchor_drift()`, retaining its offset,
common-element and uncertainty limitations. Keep the full `linked` object
when saving the analysis, so its fitted model and supplied anchors stay together.

### Limits that matter before using real data

- **Whole-facet centering includes anchors.** Unless a facet is
  `noncenter_facet`, `centering_scope = "facet"` makes all its levels sum to
  zero. With R01 = 0.70, the other ungrouped raters sum to -0.70; a single
  remaining rater is fixed at -0.70. Group totals also contribute. Incompatible
  totals stop before fitting, even when `anchor_policy = "silent"`.
  `centering_scope = "remainder"` reproduces the earlier restriction that the
  ungrouped, unanchored levels sum to zero. Saved results are not converted by
  reloading them; fitting under a different convention requires re-estimation.
  For ordinary additive RSM/PCM JML, `centering_scope = "anchor_origin"`
  instead lets direct or group anchors replace their facet's centering, as FACETS does.
  Choose an unanchored, active noncenter facet and repeat the same arithmetic
  mean target for each group member. This does not change the default or
  account for estimated-anchor error.
- **The helper does not copy every setting.** The model, estimation method,
  centering convention and MML integration mode are inherited automatically.
  Older baselines without convention metadata retain `"remainder"`.
  Repeat the intended category policy, rubric, orientation, PCM/GPCM roles,
  uncentered facet and population model. RSM/PCM MML without a population model
  fixes ability to a standard-normal distribution; it does not estimate a
  changed cohort mean/variance. An explicitly requested
  `population_formula = ~ 1` estimates normal-population moments and needs
  `person_data`; see `help("fit_mfrm")` for its assumptions.
- **Person anchors require JML.** Current MML integrates ability and rejects
  fixed Person values or Person group means. Common Persons can be present in
  the design without being anchored. Choosing JML changes the estimator and
  should follow the analysis question, not merely avoid an error.
- **Anchor uncertainty is conditional.** The new fit treats supplied values as
  exact. It does not propagate their source estimation error; an unavailable
  SE for a fixed value does not mean its source was perfectly known. Compare
  defensible anchor sets when conclusions depend on that choice.
- **Locations are not the entire calibration.** To hold thresholds and other
  supported calibration components fixed while scoring, use
  `extract_mfrm_calibration()`, validate and freeze the saved calibration,
  then call `score_mfrm_calibration()`. See `help("mfrm_calibration_workflow")`
  for its supported models and required checks.

The [FACETS centering rules](https://www.winsteps.com/facetman/centerfacet.htm)
help distinguish an origin constraint from a fixed external value, but are not
mfrmr's partial-anchor convention. [Uto (2021, pp. 1442--1444)](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01498-x)
explains common-rater/task linking and its design dependence. That simulation
fixes generated common parameters and removes a redundant rater constraint;
its Bayesian estimation does not validate mfrmr's different constraints or
supply uncertainty propagation for estimated anchors.

## Annual speech contests with common recordings

Suppose each year's contestants give a three-minute English speech. Most
judges return and use the same rubric. Before the contest, they rate a set of
recorded speeches used in previous years. You want to know whether judges
became more severe, whether the whole panel changed its standard, and whether
the new contestant group performed differently on a common scale.

The common recordings offer a link: the performance in a fixed recording
does not improve from one year to the next. Its interpretation must still be
comparable under the rubric and viewing conditions. An unchanged time limit
or criterion name alone does not establish this. Because contestants change,
a difference between annual groups is not individual growth.

This section explains the design and the limits of current functions. A
complete recording-based annual analysis, including formal year-difference
intervals, is not yet verified in mfrmr. The teaching cohorts in the first
example above do not contain annual reratings of common recordings.

### Identify the performance, judge and rating occasion

Keep one row per individual rating on one criterion. The following IDs
illustrate identities to preserve; they are not supplied example data.

| Observation | Performance ID | Judge ID | Rating year |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Judge A rates reference video V01 in 2025 | V01 | A | 2025 |
| Judge A rates that same video in 2026 | V01 | A | 2026 |
| Judge A rates a new 2026 contestant's speech | Speech_2026_01 | A | 2026 |

Also retain criterion, score, session, training phase and video/live mode.
The same speaker giving a new speech needs a new performance ID when the
measurement target is that speech. Preserve individual ratings before
discussion or disclosure of reference scores. Consensus scores alone cannot
recover differences among judges. Include performances spanning relevant
levels and criterion profiles; there is no universal adequate recording
count. The five-common-element helper warning is not such a rule.

### Choose what is shared and what is allowed to change

In **joint calibration**, analyze years together, sharing an unknown measure
for each common recording while allowing judges' severities to vary by year.
A judge-year effect represents a particular judge in a particular year;
retain the original judge ID so these effects can later be compared. The
recording measures can be estimated rather than supplied as numerical anchors.

In **fixed-reference calibration**, use previously estimated recording
measures as fixed values for a later year and estimate that year's judge
effects. This preserves a chosen reference scale but conditions on its
estimated values. When the recordings take the Person role, current mfrmr
requires JML for direct Person anchors; MML rejects them. Sharing unknown
performance measures is a different design and does not require these anchors.
Formal JML structural intervals remain unqualified.

Returning judges should not automatically be fixed to their previous
severities when their changes are the question. A panel mean fixed separately
in every year also prevents estimating a common shift. For example, centering
away a +0.40-logit increase for all judges would leave no panel-wide increase
to report. FACETS describes group anchoring as an assumption about average
severity, not proof that the panel stayed stable
([Linacre, 2012, p. 9](https://www.winsteps.com/a/ftutorial4.pdf)).

Specify scale constraints, criterion/category stability and ability-population
assumptions together. Unrestricted year effects and judge-year effects would
overlap; freely changing criteria can also absorb a common scoring shift.
Separate fixed-standard-normal MML fits do not estimate changing cohort
means. In a joint model, do not assign conflicting Person-level year
covariates to a common recording rated in several years. Its rating occasion
is not a different underlying performance.

### Read the existing helper results for their stated purpose

| Output | What it shows | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `linked$fit$facets$others` from `anchor_to_baseline()` | Facet locations under the chosen constraints | A formal annual comparison without compatible scales and an appropriate contrast analysis |
| `linked$drift` | Whether retained fixed non-Person anchors equal the supplied values | Stability of those elements, or a drift estimate for the reference recordings |
| `drift$drift_table` from `detect_anchor_drift()` | Common-element differences after removing `LinkOffset` | Absolute panel change, or calibrated significance of the SE ratio |
| `chain$cumulative` from `build_equating_chain()` | Accumulated screened adjacent-wave offsets | Propagated uncertainty or proof of annual scale comparability |

When judges are the linking set, `detect_anchor_drift()` subtracts their
common shift. If all selected differences are +0.40 logits, `LinkOffset` is
+0.40 and every residual `Drift` is zero. This describes relative alignment,
not evidence that the panel was stable. Interpreting `LinkOffset` itself as
panel change is also unjustified without a separate scale reference.

Agreement after training, operational stability and correctness against an
expert benchmark are different outcomes. Check familiar-score memory, for
example with additional recordings not used to teach the reference scores.
If the contest is rated live but the calibration uses video, paired live/video
ratings of some performances can help assess whether the estimated severity
transfers. Repeated ratings can be dependent even when their IDs are correct.

Annual-difference uncertainty needs the covariance between the relevant
estimates, or propagation of reference-calibration uncertainty where applicable.
Adding two squared SEs assumes away covariance; marginal interval overlap is
not a test of change. Report the reference, assumptions, number of common
performances and unavailable results alongside any point comparisons.

## Which uncertainty is available with anchors?

An anchor does not make every interval unavailable. For ordinary unit-weight
RSM/PCM MML with a fixed standard-normal population and fixed-grid integration,
`mfrm_facet_intervals()` can supply model-information or cluster-sandwich
intervals for free facet locations and contrasts, subject to its checks.
They condition on the supplied anchors. A fixed target has SE zero and no
inferential bounds; this does not describe the uncertainty of its original
calibration.

If the population mean and variance are also estimated, anchored point
estimation is supported, but the native location and population interval
helpers currently exclude anchors and group constraints. Inspect
`fit$readiness$fit`: `EstimabilityState = "not_evaluated"` means the
identification review is incomplete, not that numerical optimization failed
or the model was proved unidentified. The separate
`fit$data_review$estimability$nonlinear_local_estimability` can pass its
local-rank check while overall readiness remains under review. That local
result alone does not authorize intervals or exporting anchors for reuse.
Choose the population assumption for the assessment question, not simply
because one configuration supplies intervals.

For **one-family GPCM**, model-information and cluster-sandwich slope and
curve intervals can include fixed facet anchors or group means when their
own numerical checks pass. Use `confint(fit, parm = "slopes")` for relative slopes and
`mfrm_curve_intervals(fit, newdata)` for curves at specified ability values
and rating contexts. Their returned explanations state that source-anchor
uncertainty is excluded. Fixing a rater's location does not fix its slope,
category thresholds or entire response curve. A group mean does not fix
each member.

The restrictions differ by output. Anchored one-family GPCM currently has
no native-location or profile-slope interval route, and no portable-calibration
export. Fitted-object scoring with `predict_mfrm_units()` has separate source
and scoring checks. An available slope interval does not certify that source
for scoring: its finer-grid integration check may still fail. Explicit
`readiness_policy = "review"` retains review-only values and does not make
them operational scores. These distinctions also apply after saving results.

### Reusing an analysis saved before the centering change

Start with what you want to preserve or change. Saving a new copy does not
convert the statistical model.

| Intended task | Required action | What changes? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reopen the original fit | `readRDS()`; inspect `summary(fit, compute = "never")` and `specifications_report(fit)` | No estimates or constraints. A native fit lacking convention metadata retains legacy remainder centering. |
| Repeat the original estimation | Generate `build_mfrm_replay_script()` and run it with the original data | A new fit under the original convention, with newly evaluated readiness. |
| Adopt whole-facet centering | Refit with `centering_scope = "facet"`, preserving the intended other settings | The anchored constraints and potentially estimates, SEs and conclusions. |
| Update interval explanations or fixed-contrast derivatives | Recompute the interval object from its unchanged source fit | Derived output; no model refit is needed solely for this update. |
| Repair earlier anchored subgroup DFF | Rerun `analyze_dff()` from the baseline | Subgroup models are refitted; reading the old DFF object does not repair them. |
| Describe an old portable calibration more precisely | Re-extract from its source fit with the required checks, then validate and freeze a new artifact | Explicit constraint labels; this alone does not change its coefficients or convention. |

For a runnable illustration, create an analysis with the legacy convention
using the packaged ratings already loaded above. If you already have an old
fit file, start by reading that file instead. The example fixes a Rater
location, uses RSM with a fixed standard-normal population and keeps Person
as the uncentered facet. These choices illustrate migration; choose the
population assumption for your assessment question.

```{r migration-legacy}
migration_anchor <- data.frame(Facet = "Rater", Level = "R01", Anchor = 0.70)
legacy_fit <- fit_mfrm(
  ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  model = "RSM", method = "MML", anchors = migration_anchor,
  noncenter_facet = "Person", centering_scope = "remainder",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  quad_points = 31, maxit = 400, reltol = 1e-9
)
fit_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(legacy_fit, fit_file)
restored_fit <- readRDS(fit_file)
unlink(fit_file)
spec <- specifications_report(restored_fit)$data_spec
spec[spec$Setting %in% c("NonCenteredFacet", "CenteringScope"), ]
```

`CenteringScope = "remainder"` describes the fitted constraint, including for
native files saved before this field existed. It is not changed to the new
default merely because a newer package reads the file. Do not assign a new
value to `fit$config$centering_scope` or recenter its coefficient table: the
likelihood, parameter mapping and uncertainty still belong to the original fit.

To change the convention, fit a **separate model** from the original responses.
Here only the declared centering changes. Inspect its numerical and design
status; the number of quadrature points is not an accuracy guarantee.

```{r migration-whole-facet}
updated_fit <- fit_mfrm(
  ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  model = "RSM", method = "MML", anchors = migration_anchor,
  noncenter_facet = "Person", centering_scope = "facet",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  quad_points = 31, maxit = 400, reltol = 1e-9
)
summary(updated_fit, compute = "never", detail = "brief")
old_raters <- subset(restored_fit$facets$others, Facet == "Rater")
new_raters <- subset(updated_fit$facets$others, Facet == "Rater")
data.frame(
  Convention = c("remainder", "facet"),
  FixedR01 = c(old_raters$Estimate[old_raters$Level == "R01"],
               new_raters$Estimate[new_raters$Level == "R01"]),
  OtherRaterSum = c(sum(old_raters$Estimate[old_raters$Level != "R01"]),
                    sum(new_raters$Estimate[new_raters$Level != "R01"]))
)
```

Both fits keep R01 at 0.70. The remaining raters sum to zero in the legacy
fit and -0.70 in the whole-facet fit. This changes R01's comparison with the
other raters; it is not just a renamed column. Retain the two analyses under
different filenames, and report the convention with the other model settings.
Complete facet anchors can also become incompatible with a whole-facet zero
sum. Resolve that model specification explicitly rather than rounding anchors
or silently switching the population model.

For more complex analyses, `build_mfrm_replay_script(restored_fit,
data_file = "ratings.csv")` provides a recipe with stored anchors, group means
and the original convention. It requires the original analysis data at the
specified path. Review its generated `fit_mfrm()` call before deliberately
changing the convention; preserve population covariates, category handling,
orientation, uncentered facets and PCM/GPCM owners. This recipe **refits**.
By contrast, the replay written by `export_mfrm_results()` reopens its saved
results bundle without reconstructing the model.

If only a frozen calibration survives, retain its original scoring meaning.
Generic old identification labels are insufficient to infer its centering
convention. See `vignette("mfrmr-portable-calibration", package = "mfrmr")`
for re-extraction and validation; changing a label is not recalibration.
Earlier MML fits containing Person anchors require special review because
those values were ignored. Current fitting rejects them; choosing
`centering_scope = "remainder"` does not repair that earlier analysis.

### Comparing an anchor with TAM or ConQuest

An anchor is a fixed value in all three programs, but **the surrounding
constraints determine what that value means**. Copying a number from another
program is insufficient when its parameterization or population model differs.

| Question | mfrmr | TAM | ConQuest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What is fixed? | A named facet location in `anchors` | Indexed response-design coefficients in `xsi.fixed` | Response-design coefficients imported with `anchor_parameters` / `anchor_xsi` |
| Are steps and slopes included automatically? | No; the location-anchor table omits them | Check the response and scoring designs; slope controls are separate | Check the response design and scoring parameters; `anchor_tau` is separate |
| How is the population specified? | Ordinary RSM/PCM MML defaults to fixed standard-normal ability; population modeling is explicit | Specify `beta.fixed`, `variance.fixed` and the selected fitting function's other controls | Specify population anchors and location/scale constraints explicitly |
| Can Person values be fixed? | Supported in JML; rejected in MML | `tam.jml()` documents `theta.fixed` for `version = 1` | The manual states that `anchor_theta` is ignored in MML |

The [TAM MML documentation](https://alexanderrobitzsch.github.io/TAM/reference/tam.mml.html),
[TAM JML documentation](https://alexanderrobitzsch.github.io/TAM/reference/tam.jml.html)
and [ConQuest command reference](https://conquestmanual.acer.org/s4-00.html)
describe these controls. For ConQuest, read `import` together with `set`;
importing anchors alone does not specify all location and scale constraints.
Parameter indices must be checked against the actual model design and retained
levels. A changed index can fix the wrong coefficient without a syntax error.

For example, let four rater severities be \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_4\),
with R01 fixed at \(\gamma_1=0.70\), and no group constraints:

| Constraint choice | Remaining raters | R01 minus the mean of the remaining raters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mfrmr legacy `centering_scope = "remainder"` | \(\gamma_2+\gamma_3+\gamma_4=0\) | 0.70 |
| mfrmr default `centering_scope = "facet"` | \(\gamma_1+\gamma_2+\gamma_3+\gamma_4=0\), hence the remaining sum is -0.70 | \(0.70-(-0.70/3)\), approximately 0.933 |

The second row applies, for example, to TAM's
`tam.mml.mfr(formulaA = ~ item + rater + step, constraint = "cases")`
and ConQuest's `model task+rater+step` with `lconstraints=cases`.
Those settings also leave the first task term uncentered, unlike mfrmr's
default. These are specific model configurations, not universal software
conventions. The different rater contrasts show why applying the same anchor
and then shifting the final locations is not generally an equivalent analysis.
Group-mean anchors need corresponding linear constraints; fixing every member
to the group mean would impose a different model.

For unit-slope RSM/PCM with all facet locations centered and an estimated
population mean \(\mu\), another equivalent origin uses a zero population mean
and uncentered task locations: set \(\theta'=\theta-\mu\) and
\(b'_{task}=b_{task}-\mu\). Rater severities, centered step ladders and
population variance stay the same, so every response probability is unchanged.
This mapping applies to the configuration with Rater anchors above. If a task
value is also anchored, its constraint must be transformed with it. In
particular, estimating population variance and fixing it to one are different
models; moving the origin does not reconcile that difference. Checking this
mapping is distinct from running and comparing both programs' optimizers.

To compare programs, first match the ratings, category coding, response
probabilities, free and fixed parameters, and population assumptions. A
coordinate transformation must carry the anchors and population parameters
with it. Then check numerical integration and optimization. Finally compare
SEs for the same parameter or contrast, transforming the covariance matrix
when coordinates differ. A point-estimate match alone does not validate an
uncertainty method or include source-anchor uncertainty.

A bounded check using all 48 Persons, four raters and four criteria in
`example_core` illustrates both outcomes. Under the whole-rater constraint
above, TAM 4.3.25 and ConQuest 5.47.5 agreed to within \(3.1\times10^{-6}\)
in their free response-design coefficients. A separate explicit TAM design
representing mfrmr's legacy remainder constraints agreed with that mode to within
\(1.8\times10^{-7}\), when mfrmr used 81-point Gauss--Hermite integration.
Both comparisons fixed ability to \(N(0,1)\). For the latter comparison,
31-point integration in that legacy mode left a maximum coefficient difference
of about 0.00067; increasing integration precision resolved it. Equal node
counts across programs do not guarantee equal quadrature rules or accuracy.

This checks one RSM configuration and its point estimates, not general
compatibility for PCM, GPCM, group constraints, JML or SEs. It does not make
81 points a universal requirement. More importantly, being able to reproduce
mfrmr's restricted model in another program does not establish that its
partial-anchor constraints answer a particular linking question. Decide which
locations and population moments should remain free before choosing the model.

## Fit and diagnose the observed ratings

```{r setup}
library(mfrmr)

bias_df <- load_mfrmr_data("example_bias")

fit <- fit_mfrm(
  bias_df,
  person = "Person",
  facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score",
  method = "MML",
  model = "RSM",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve"
)

diag <- diagnose_mfrm(fit, residual_pca = "none")
```

## 1. Check connectedness first

Use `subset_connectivity_report()` before interpreting subgroup or cross-form
contrasts.

```{r connectivity, fig.alt = "Observed rating connections across design subsets. Disconnected blocks indicate where a common measurement scale needs additional linking evidence."}
sc <- subset_connectivity_report(fit, diagnostics = diag)

sc$summary[, c("Subset", "Observations", "ObservationPercent")]
plot(sc, type = "design_matrix", preset = "publication")
```

Interpretation:

- Sparse rows or columns indicate weaker design coverage.
- Weak coverage should lower confidence in subgroup comparisons.
- Use the co-observation design graph, not rater agreement,
  severity-direction, or halo response networks, to assess empirical
  connectedness. Response-network correlations do not create a common scale.

## 2. Export anchor candidates

`make_anchor_table()` mechanically exports fitted values in the direct-anchor
schema. Its output is a candidate table, not a validated anchor set.

```{r anchors}
anchors <- make_anchor_table(fit, facets = "Criterion")
head(anchors)
```

By default, `make_anchor_table()` refuses a source whose current readiness
record does not have `InferenceReady = TRUE`. Use
`readiness_policy = "review"` only to inspect review-only candidate values, not
to reuse them as anchors. For a ready reference fit, also document cross-run
element identity and invariance and confirm compatible model, score,
orientation, and population conventions. Then use `review_mfrm_anchors()` to
check table syntax and receiving-data support. That review does not certify the
substantive link.

Keep the roles distinct: common ratings or common elements supply observed
design overlap; `anchors` fix individual parameters; `group_anchors` constrain
a group mean under an externally justified target or equal-mean assumption.
Neither constraint type manufactures empirical overlap.

### Design the link, not only the percentage

No anchor percentage or count is universally adequate. In sparse designs,
link quality also depends on coverage, the distribution and redundancy of the
links, whether one articulation point or critical edge holds the network
together, the location and model fit of the linking set, and the intended use
of ranks or classifications. Inspect both Rater-centered and Person/task-
centered assignment graphs rather than treating a minimum count as proof of a
common scale. This distinction is consistent with work on sparse linking
networks by [Myford and Wolfe (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2000.tb01832.x),
[Wind and Jones (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164417703733), and
[Uto (2021)](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01498-x).

Fixed anchor values also carry uncertainty from their source calibration.
Current mfrmr drift and chain summaries do not propagate every source-fit,
offset, and cross-fit covariance component. When results depend on the anchor
set, compare defensible alternatives and report that sensitivity.
[Robitzsch (2024, pp. 1181--1182, 1187--1188)](https://doi.org/10.3390/appliedmath4030063)
examines a different source of linking error: random uniform DIF in fixed-item
2PL calibration. Its derivation neglects Person sampling error and does not
provide a variance estimator for fitted population parameters. It supports
checking invariance, not claiming that mfrmr propagates all linking uncertainty.

## 3. Compare group residuals

Residual comparisons describe how observed-minus-expected scores differ
between groups. They use score units and do not test differential functioning.

A group with higher average ability can score higher without differential
functioning. DFF concerns a facet difference at the same ability. Residual
screens inherit the fitted population assumptions, and fixed-standard-normal
RSM/PCM subgroup refits do not estimate group ability distributions. Linking
anchors alone do not address an omitted group difference. Review these
assumptions before interpreting a residual difference involving a rater
or criterion.

Representing group ability differences is necessary for a suitable population
model, but does not turn the current residual screen into a calibrated DFF
test. MML residuals evaluate expected scores at EAP ability estimates. Because
the response function is nonlinear, a no-DFF model can still have different
mean residuals across groups. This concerns the null being tested as well as
its standard error.

The residual method therefore returns no p-values, confidence intervals or
positive/negative classifications. For compatibility, its former SE and test
columns contain `NA`. Recompute older residual results with `analyze_dff()`
using the existing fit and original data; no model refit is needed.

```{r dff-residual, fig.alt = "Ordered criterion contrasts in mean observed-minus-expected scores, Group1 minus Group2. These descriptive differences are in score units, without confidence intervals or a formal DFF decision."}
dff_resid <- analyze_dff(
  fit,
  diag,
  facet = "Criterion",
  group = "Group",
  data = bias_df,
  method = "residual"
)

screen <- plot(dff_resid, type = "summary")
comparisons <- plot_data(screen, "pairs")
comparisons[, c("Level", "Group1", "Group2", "Contrast",
                "N_Group1", "N_Group2", "PlotStatus")]
```

Read the figure and this table together:

1. The labels follow `Level | Group1 | Group2`. `Contrast` subtracts the
   residual mean of Group2 from that of Group1. A positive value means higher
   residual scores in Group1, not established leniency, favoritism or unfairness.
2. `N_Group1` and `N_Group2` count retained ratings, not independent Persons.
   Repeated ratings can make these counts large even when few Persons contribute.
   The same table has `NPersons_Group1` and `NPersons_Group2` for distinct Persons.
3. `PlotStatus` separates displayed comparisons from finite comparisons omitted
   by `top_n` and comparisons with unavailable contrasts. None of these display
   states is a DFF decision. For an unavailable row, inspect `sparse` and the
   counts: the residual pairwise contrast requires both cells to meet `min_obs`.
   An absent group has a count of zero, not a zero difference.

Check how the requested ratings matched the fitted responses. This matters
before comparing screens from different data subsets:

```{r dff-response-support}
cases <- plot_data(screen, "cases")
table(cases$Reason)
cases[!cases$Included, ]
plot_data(screen, "notes")
```

`InputRow` identifies a row of the supplied data; `FitRow` identifies its
matched fitted response. Exclusion reasons distinguish a missing group, an
invalid/missing response, and a response absent from the fitted data. A fully
matched example has no excluded rows; this does not establish independence.
Response exclusions and unavailable *comparisons* are different stages.

For a grid of the same pairwise differences, use
`plot(dff_resid, type = "heatmap", metric = "contrast")`. The default heatmap
instead shows each group's mean observed-minus-expected score. That cell mean
can appear even below `min_obs`; read its saved `pairs$sparse` and counts.
The scaled-residual (`metric = "t"`) and pairwise-contrast routes withhold
values below this threshold. Missing cells/contrasts stay missing, not zero.
If every contrast is unavailable, inspect `dff_resid$dif_table` or the contrast
heatmap; the summary has no finite points to draw.

Reserve `ScaleLinkStatus` and `ContrastComparable` for refit-based contrasts;
their residual-method values do not describe a failed link.

## 4. Refit DFF when subgroup comparisons are defensible

The refit route reports logit-scale point contrasts when subgroup linking
supports a common scale. Any available SE or test statistic conditions on the
baseline anchors and omits their uncertainty and cross-refit covariance;
`FormalInferenceEligible` remains `FALSE`, even with adequate linking.
The default refit linking screen requires at least five anchored levels in
total across the non-target linking facets in each subgroup. A weak link
withholds contrast SEs and p-values. Inspect `LinkingAnchoredLevels`,
`LinkingThreshold`, and `ScaleLinkStatus`; five is a local screening threshold,
not a universal adequate anchor count or proof of invariance. It differs from
the per-facet common-element screen called `LinkSupportAdequate` in drift and
link-review results.

Direct anchors on the target facet and JML Person anchors remain fixed during
subgroup refits. Check `Fixed1` and `Fixed2`: when either is true, the row
retains its estimates but has no contrast, SE or test. Supplying the same
rater severity in both groups cannot establish that the rater functions
equally across groups. Residual DFF can describe response departures under
those constraints. To estimate a free target contrast, explicitly fit a
baseline with the intended target constraints first. Older saved refit DFF
objects may have dropped target or Person anchors; rerun `analyze_dff()` from
the baseline fit to obtain subgroup estimates under the corrected rule.
Loading an old result does not change it.

Check `ComparisonStatus` and `ComparisonReason` before interpreting a number.
A failed or skipped subgroup fit has no subgroup estimate; the baseline value
is not a replacement. An absent target level remains in the comparison table
with a missing contrast. `N_Group1` / `N_Group2` count retained responses for
that target level, while `N_Subgroup1` / `N_Subgroup2` count all retained
responses in the subgroup. Failed fits have unknown retained counts, not zero;
their input counts remain in `$group_fits[[group]]$N_Input`.

Sparse cells, missing SEs and Persons shared across the two subgroup fits
withhold the independent-subgroup screen. Actual point estimates remain
available, and `ConditionalScreenReason` explains missing uncertainty.
Disjoint Person IDs alone do not establish independence or valid matching.
The Welch degrees of freedom use response counts and are only a screening
approximation. Older refit objects must be recomputed from the baseline and
original data before using current summary, report or plotting methods;
regenerate their exported tables and figures as well.

Bias screening answers a different question: `estimate_bias()` estimates
an additional shift for each cell while holding the calibration fixed. A
positive `Bias Size` raises the expected score. An anchored rater can still
have a nonzero cell shift and a conditional SE for that shift. This SE does
not include uncertainty in the fitted calibration or the supplied anchors,
and it is not a joint-interaction confidence interval. `Obs-Exp Average`
is the observed-minus-expected average under the baseline calibration, before
fitting the shift. `AfterBiasObsExpAverage` records the remaining discrepancy
with that shift included. Both are on the score scale; `Bias Size` is in logits.

Refits currently refuse baselines with user-specified active population
models, fitted facet interactions, or group-anchor constraints because those
structures cannot yet be replayed and linked completely within subgroups.
The default GPCM-MML identification intercept is handled separately. Residual
DFF remains a screening alternative; see `?analyze_dff` for the exact scope.

```{r dff-refit}
dff_refit <- analyze_dff(
  fit,
  diag,
  facet = "Criterion",
  group = "Group",
  data = bias_df,
  method = "refit"
)

dff_refit$summary
dff_refit$dif_table[, c("Level", "Group1", "Group2", "Contrast",
                       "ScaleLinkStatus", "Fixed1", "Fixed2")]
dff_refit$dif_table[, c("Level", "LinkingAnchoredLevels1",
                       "LinkingAnchoredLevels2", "LinkingThreshold")]
```

Here `Contrast` still means Group1 minus Group2, but its units are **logits**.
A positive value means a larger facet location in Group1. Holding other
parameters fixed, the usual difficulty/severity orientation lowers expected
scores. Subgroup step ladders or slopes can also differ, so location alone
does not order the entire response curves. `ContrastDirection` records larger,
smaller or equal locations, including for positive-orientation facets.
Check the model's facet signs and score coding. Do not compare the sign as if it had
the residual method's meaning, or put the two methods on a shared effect axis.
Read `LinkingDetail1` and `LinkingDetail2` when linking support is weak.
A plotted finite contrast does not by itself establish a common scale;
even `ScaleLinkStatus = "linked"` does not qualify formal inference.

For schools with separate rater panels, common recordings can connect joint
calibration while a particular rater still lacks observations in one school.
That connection alone cannot identify that rater's school contrast. Keep a
common recording's identity across ratings; do not duplicate it as independent
school participants to manufacture a comparison.

### Review a particular school comparison before fitting

The question is whether the rating assignments identify the requested
interaction contrast, rather than merely connect the panels. This small
constructed assignment isolates that question: R4 rates School A only,
while the other raters rate both origins. The scores only supply the declared
three-category format; they are not evidence for a school effect, and eight
performances are not a recommended sample size.

```{r school-comparison-review}
school_ratings <- expand.grid(
  Person = paste0("P", 1:8), Rater = paste0("R", 1:4),
  Criterion = c("C1", "C2"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
school_ratings$School <- ifelse(
  school_ratings$Person %in% paste0("P", 1:4), "A", "B"
)
school_ratings$Score <- (as.integer(factor(school_ratings$Person)) +
  as.integer(factor(school_ratings$Rater)) +
  as.integer(factor(school_ratings$Criterion))) %% 3
school_ratings <- subset(school_ratings, !(Rater == "R4" & School == "B"))

school_questions <- list(
  facet = "Rater", group = "School", groups = c("A", "B"),
  model = "RSM", method = "JML",
  contrasts = rbind(
    R1_vs_panel = c(R1 = .75, R2 = -.25, R3 = -.25, R4 = -.25),
    R1_vs_R2 = c(R1 = 1, R2 = -1, R3 = 0, R4 = 0)
  )
)
school_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  school_ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "School"), "Score",
  rating_min = 0, rating_max = 2, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE, comparisons = school_questions
)
school_review$comparison_review$table[, c(
  "Comparison", "Group1", "Group2", "State", "N_Group1", "N_Group2"
)]
school_review$comparison_review$cells
```

Each row applies its weights to the raters' **A-minus-B interaction effects**.
`R1_vs_panel` subtracts the equal-weight average across all four raters;
`R1_vs_R2` subtracts R2's school difference from R1's. The first is
`target_unidentified`, while the second is `target_identified_only`.
R4's missing B ratings matter to the whole-panel reference. Dropping R4 and
renormalizing weights would answer a different question.

The `IdentificationBasis` column makes the role of assumptions explicit.
For the same ratings and target weights, compare a common normal ability
population with a normal regression allowing school-specific means. These
reviews do not estimate either model:

```{r school-comparison-assumptions}
population_reviews <- lapply(
  list(common_normal = ~1, school_means = ~School),
  function(population) {
    question <- school_questions
    question$method <- "MML"
    question$population_formula <- population
    describe_mfrm_data(
      school_ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "School"), "Score",
      rating_min = 0, rating_max = 2, category_policy = "preserve",
      include_agreement = FALSE, comparisons = question
    )$comparison_review
  }
)
lapply(population_reviews, function(review) review$table[, c(
  "Comparison", "ConditionalState", "FreePersonState", "IdentificationBasis", "State"
)])
```

For `R1_vs_panel`, the common normal model reports `population_restriction`:
the unrestricted-Person ambiguity disappears only after imposing that model's
population restrictions. Allowing school-specific means restores the ambiguity,
so the basis is `unidentified`. No additional rating was observed in either
review. The common population assumption is substantive; it is not a harmless
change of coordinates or evidence that the missing R4/B ratings exist.

For `R1_vs_R2`, both models report `free_person_response_model`: the declared
response map identifies this target even with unrestricted Person locations.
That statement still assumes the response model, including its slope and step
restrictions. It does not make an MML estimate distribution-free. Both positive
MML conditional results keep `State = "not_evaluated"`, because the review
does not prove global marginal identification. Read `IdentificationDetail`
and the review's `notes` before selecting a model; a more convenient result is
not a reason to assume equal ability populations.

The declared response model includes a zero-valued School main facet and a
zero-margin Rater-by-School interaction, alongside free JML Person locations.
Its settings are saved in `school_review$comparison_review$fit_arguments`.
The review does not fit this rank-deficient model, estimate the identified
contrast, or supply an interval. The ordinary full-fit guard still refuses
the model. Identification of one target is not permission to set other effects
to arbitrary values and report the resulting estimates.

Adding genuinely shared recordings from both origins can supply missing
comparisons. Keep each recording's original Person and School labels across
raters. Neutral recordings may connect the measurement scale without filling
the missing A/B interaction information. PCM reviews also require an explicit
step owner. GPCM does not currently support this interaction model and is
reported as `unsupported`; its separate slope/product qualifications cannot
be substituted for this school review.

### Preserve that question alongside a residual screen

For the bundled data used above, explicitly request an MML prospective
Rater-by-Group review, then attach it to a residual screen of the same ratings.
The model in this review is a prospective interaction model; the fitted
screening model remains the earlier additive RSM. No interaction fit is
silently added.

```{r dff-comparison-review}
rater_levels <- sort(unique(as.character(bias_df$Rater)))
panel_weights <- matrix(-1 / length(rater_levels), 1, length(rater_levels),
  dimnames = list("First rater versus panel", rater_levels))
panel_weights[1, 1] <- panel_weights[1, 1] + 1
prospective <- describe_mfrm_data(
  bias_df, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Group"), "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE,
  comparisons = list(facet = "Rater", group = "Group", groups = c("A", "B"),
    contrasts = panel_weights, model = "RSM", method = "MML")
)
rater_screen <- analyze_dff(
  fit, facet = "Rater", group = "Group", data = bias_df,
  comparison_review = prospective
)
summary(rater_screen)$comparison_review$table
support <- plot(rater_screen, draw = FALSE)
plot_data(support, "comparison_review")$weights
report <- dif_report(rater_screen)
report$comparison_review$table
saveRDS(rater_screen, file.path(tempdir(), "rater-screen-with-review.rds"))
```

Positive `ConditionalState` values concern the conditional linear response
map. Under MML, `State = "not_evaluated"` deliberately withholds a positive
global marginal-identification claim; it does not mean the residual calculation
failed. A proven same-conditional-law ambiguity can still produce
`target_unidentified` after mixing. `FreePersonState` and `Basis` expose the
population assumption separately. Neither rank nor a finite residual difference
qualifies a DFF test. The attached review keeps all requested rows, weights,
counts and limitations; it does not replace the residual table with structural
parameter estimates. Changed rating subsets or origin assignments require a
new review before attachment.

### Estimate the declared contrast in one joint calibration

When the assignment supports the whole model, the next question is the size
of the specified interaction contrast in a joint fit. Use the bundled
`example_bias` ratings from the screen above. Its Group labels illustrate
the origin role; this synthetic example is not evidence about actual schools.
Allow Group-specific population means through `~Group`, so an equal-population
restriction is not silently used to explain the group difference. School/Group
remains a zero main facet; the population mean and rater-by-group interaction
have separate roles.

The first comparison is the first rater's A-minus-B interaction relative to
the equal-weight whole panel. The second subtracts the second rater's A-minus-B
interaction. This compares school differences, not the raters' overall severity.

```{r joint-comparison-estimates}
joint_questions <- prospective$comparison_review$specification
joint_questions$population_formula <- ~Group
pair_weights <- setNames(rep(0, length(rater_levels)), rater_levels)
pair_weights[1:2] <- c(1, -1)
joint_questions$contrasts <- rbind(
  panel_weights, "First versus second rater" = pair_weights
)
joint_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  bias_df, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Group"), "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE, comparisons = joint_questions
)
joint_fit <- do.call(fit_mfrm, c(
  list(data = bias_df, quad_points = 63L),
  joint_review$comparison_review$fit_arguments
))
joint_results <- summary(joint_fit, comparison_review = joint_review)
joint_comparisons <- joint_results$interaction_comparisons
joint_comparisons[, c(
  "Comparison", "Group1", "Group2", "Estimate", "EstimateStatus",
  "State", "ConditionalState", "QuadratureState", "FormalInferenceEligible"
)]
attr(joint_comparisons, "fit_checks")$numerical
attr(joint_comparisons, "comparison_review")$weights
saveRDS(list(fit = joint_fit, review = joint_review, results = joint_results),
  file.path(tempdir(), "joint-school-comparisons.rds"))
```

The two fitted contrasts are approximately **0.58** and **0.92 logits**.
A positive value indicates the weighted relative shift toward higher coded
scores for A versus B under this model. It is not an absolute advantage for
School A, a comparison of population means, or proof of unfairness. The
values differ from the earlier residual-screen statistic because that statistic
asks a different question.

`interaction_effect_table(joint_fit, comparison_review = joint_review)` returns
the same comparison table directly. Without `comparison_review`, it continues
to return individual interaction cells. The numerical checks reevaluate the
saved joint likelihood and full gradient without optimization. For this
example, 31-node fixed quadrature did not meet the finer-grid check; 63 nodes
were selected after checking agreement with 127. This order is not a universal
accuracy recommendation. `QuadratureState = "stable_at_retained_point"` means
the retained point passed the specified integration check, not that the model
or its uncertainty has been validated.

`EstimateStatus = "descriptive_only"` keeps the fitted value separate from
identification and inference. Positive conditional MML ranks still retain
`State = "not_evaluated"`; this example does not prove global marginal
identification. Inspect `FitReadiness`, `BoundaryState`, `NumericalState`,
`EstimateReason` and the saved checks. A failed check leaves `Estimate` missing;
`OptimizerEstimate` is then only a numerical trace. This extraction table supplies
no SEs, confidence limits or formal tests. The separate interval example below
uses `mfrm_facet_intervals(comparison_review = ...)` with additional joint-information
and finer-grid checks. Keep the full saved object to preserve weights,
empty cells, population assumptions and checks; a CSV does not retain these
attributes.

### Estimate an identified comparison when the full model is deficient

Suppose the last rater has no ratings from Group B. The first-versus-second
rater comparison can still be identified, but the comparison with the whole
panel includes an unobserved rater/group cell. An ordinary full fit correctly
refuses this deficient design. Explicit comparison-only estimation can retain
the observed likelihood and estimate its invariant targets without reporting
arbitrary values for the unidentifiable interaction cells.

This example uses **JML with free Person locations**. It does not assume equal
normal populations across groups. It uses the same declared interaction target
as before, on the reduced assignment, but changes the estimator and the
observed ratings; its numerical value is therefore not a replication of the
preceding full-design MML value.

```{r partial-comparison-estimates}
incomplete_ratings <- bias_df[!(bias_df$Rater == tail(rater_levels, 1) &
                                bias_df$Group == "B"), ]
partial_questions <- joint_questions
partial_questions$method <- "JML"
partial_questions$population_formula <- NULL
partial_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  incomplete_ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Group"), "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE, comparisons = partial_questions
)
partial_fit <- do.call(fit_mfrm, c(
  list(data = incomplete_ratings, fit_scope = "comparisons",
       comparison_review = partial_review, interaction_policy = "silent"),
  partial_review$comparison_review$fit_arguments
))
partial_comparisons <- interaction_effect_table(partial_fit)
partial_comparisons[, c(
  "Comparison", "ConditionalState", "Estimate", "EstimateStatus",
  "BoundaryState", "NumericalState", "EstimateReason"
)]
partial_fit$checks$numerical
saveRDS(partial_fit, file.path(tempdir(), "partial-school-comparisons.rds"))
```

The whole-panel comparison remains **missing**; the first-versus-second rater
contrast is approximately **1.08 logits**, with `target_identified_only` and
`descriptive_only`. This is an A-minus-B difference between those two raters'
interaction effects. It does not recover the missing last-rater/B effect.
`summary(partial_fit)` returns the same table. This dedicated result cannot be
used as an ordinary full model for Person scoring or individual-cell inference.

Identifiability alone is insufficient. For JML, the comparison route uses
`lpSolve` to check whether any parameter direction can increase the likelihood
without reaching a finite maximum. A detected or unchecked recession withholds
all estimates, even if some contrasts might have limits in an extended model;
that extension is outside this route. Failed convergence, insufficient reduced
curvature or unsupported categories also retain missing values and reasons.

For MML, declare its population model in the review before fitting. The same
coordinate reduction preserves every conditional probability and the marginal
likelihood. Multiple starting variances and finer quadrature assess numerical
adequacy; they do not prove global marginal identification or a unique global
maximum. Positive conditional results still keep `State = "not_evaluated"`.
Neither route supplies SEs, confidence intervals or formal DFF tests. The
saved `representation` and `optimization` are audit coordinates, not reportable
cell parameters. See `?fit_mfrm` for the supported scope and acceptance criteria.

### Obtain CML uncertainty for the identified comparison

For the same incomplete assignment, CML conditions on each Person's total
score. It needs no ability distribution and avoids estimating one incidental
ability parameter per Person. The inferential target remains the declared
rater-by-origin interaction contrast. Start with the bundled synthetic ratings
and specify the two comparisons explicitly:

```{r partial-cml-comparisons}
cml_data <- load_mfrmr_data("example_bias")
cml_raters <- sort(unique(as.character(cml_data$Rater)))
cml_ratings <- cml_data[!(cml_data$Rater == tail(cml_raters, 1) &
                          cml_data$Group == "B"), ]
cml_weights <- rbind(
  panel = c(1, rep(0, length(cml_raters) - 1)) - 1 / length(cml_raters),
  pair = c(1, -1, rep(0, length(cml_raters) - 2))
)
colnames(cml_weights) <- cml_raters
cml_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  cml_ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Group"), "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE,
  comparisons = list(facet = "Rater", group = "Group", groups = c("A", "B"),
                     contrasts = cml_weights, model = "RSM", method = "CML")
)
cml_fit <- do.call(fit_mfrm, c(
  list(data = cml_ratings, fit_scope = "comparisons",
       comparison_review = cml_review, interaction_policy = "silent"),
  cml_review$comparison_review$fit_arguments
))
cml_table <- interaction_effect_table(cml_fit)
cml_table[, c("Comparison", "ConditionalState", "Estimate", "SE", "Lower",
              "Upper", "FormalInferenceEligible", "EstimateReason")]
cml_fit$covariance
saveRDS(cml_fit, file.path(tempdir(), "cml-school-comparisons.rds"))
```

Read the `pair` row: the estimated contrast is approximately **0.925 logits**,
SE **0.518**, with a pointwise 95% Wald interval of **−0.090 to 1.939**.
It is the first rater's A-minus-B interaction minus the second rater's
A-minus-B interaction. The interval includes zero. The `panel` estimate,
SE and limits remain `NA`, because its weights involve the missing last-rater/B
cell. Zero-filling that row would change the inferential claim. The full
contrast covariance is retained in `cml_fit$covariance`, including missing
entries for unavailable targets; `summary(cml_fit)` returns the same table.

Reuse that fit through the same interval interface used for full models.
No estimation or information calculation is repeated. The missing `panel`
comparison stays in the display as "not estimated", with no point or interval:

```{r partial-cml-interval-display, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="CML rater-by-origin contrasts: the pair estimate has a pointwise 95 percent conditional-information interval; the unidentified panel row is labeled not estimated and has no point."}
cml_intervals <- mfrm_facet_intervals(cml_fit)
plot(cml_intervals)
apa_table(cml_intervals, which = "intervals")$table
saveRDS(cml_intervals, file.path(tempdir(), "cml-school-intervals.rds"))
```

Use `mfrm_facet_intervals(cml_fit, level = .90)` for pointwise 90% limits;
only the normal critical value changes. The saved `comparison_review` retains
the group order, weights and empty cells, and `fit_checks` retains the numerical
qualification. `apa_table(cml_intervals, which = "comparison_cells")` shows
which crossings were observed. These dedicated CML objects are not ordinary
`mfrm_results()` fits and do not enable Person scoring or full-model diagnostics.

CML identification uses all possible patterns at the **observed totals**,
not just the unconditional response design. Extreme-total Persons contribute
no information. The fit removes unidentified directions only from its internal
coordinates, then checks finite-MLE existence, convergence and the full
conditional information in the identified subspace. A recession or failed
check withholds inference with a reason. For PCM, declare `model = "PCM"` and
its `step_facet` in the review before fitting.

The intervals are asymptotic under a correct response model, independent
Persons, fixed structural dimension and increasing information. Numerical
agreement with independent calculations is not a finite-sample coverage
study for every school design. These estimates do not establish a calibrated
DFF classification or recover Person abilities or between-group ability means.
CML estimates **no population SD**, so it cannot supply a contrast divided by
that fit's estimated ability SD. The separate MML standardization uses its
joint delta method, including uncertainty and cross-covariance for the fitted
SD. Save the whole CML object as RDS to retain weights, checks and missing-cell
information; CSV exports only the displayed columns.

### Standardize an MML interaction contrast by that fit's population SD

A contrast in logits and a contrast in ability-population SD units answer
different questions. For the latter, define the denominator using the **same
fit** that estimates the interaction. The following example uses the complete
`example_bias` assignment and explicitly assumes one common normal ability
population through `population_formula = ~1`. This differs from the preceding
MML example with `~Group`, which allowed group-specific means, and from the
incomplete CML example. The change is a modeling assumption, not just a display
option; do not replace `~Group` with `~1` solely to obtain a standardized result.

```{r standardized-interaction-intervals, warning=FALSE}
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_bias")
raters <- sort(unique(as.character(ratings$Rater)))
weights <- rbind(
  panel = c(1, rep(0, length(raters) - 1)) - 1 / length(raters),
  pair = c(1, -1, rep(0, length(raters) - 2))
)
colnames(weights) <- raters
sd_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Group"), "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, category_policy = "preserve",
  include_agreement = FALSE,
  comparisons = list(facet = "Rater", group = "Group", groups = c("A", "B"),
    contrasts = weights, model = "RSM", method = "MML", population_formula = ~1)
)
sd_fit <- do.call(fit_mfrm, c(
  list(data = ratings, quad_points = 63, interaction_policy = "silent"),
  sd_review$comparison_review$fit_arguments
))
sd_intervals <- mfrm_facet_intervals(
  sd_fit, comparison_review = sd_review, scale = "standardized"
)
sd_intervals$settings$population_sd
summary(sd_intervals)[, c("Target", "NativeEstimate", "Estimate", "SE", "Lower", "Upper")]
saveRDS(sd_intervals, file.path(tempdir(), "standardized-school-intervals.rds"))
```

Here the fitted SD is approximately **0.976**. The first-minus-second rater's
A-minus-B interaction is **0.927 logits**, or **0.950 population SD units**,
with SE **0.494** and a pointwise 95% interval of **−0.018 to 1.918**.
The interval includes zero. `NativeEstimate` keeps the original scale alongside
the standardized result, and `covariance` retains covariance between the two
requested contrasts. The pointwise intervals do not adjust for selecting or
examining multiple contrasts.

For contrast $d$ and log population variance $\lambda=\log(\sigma^2)$,
$t=d/\sigma$ has derivatives $J_d/\sigma$ and $-t/2$. The implemented variance
is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat t)\approx
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat d)
 +\hat d^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\lambda)/4
 -\hat d\operatorname{Cov}(\hat d,\hat\lambda)}{\hat\sigma^2}.
$$

It uses the full joint marginal-information inverse. Dividing the native SE or
interval endpoints by $\hat\sigma$ leaves out denominator uncertainty and its
covariance with the contrast. The ratio can be unstable when the fitted SD is
near zero; standardization does not cure weak information.

```{r standardized-interaction-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="Two rater-by-origin interaction contrasts with pointwise 95 percent model-information delta-method intervals in estimated population standard-deviation units; the zero line is a reference."}
plot(sd_intervals)
```

The usual saved-results path carries the same targets, scale, checks and
review into plots, reports and table exports, without fitting again:

```{r standardized-interaction-report}
sd_results <- mfrm_results(
  sd_fit, intervals = list(school = sd_intervals),
  include = c("fit", "plots"), compute = "never"
)
sd_results$tables$facet_school_intervals[, c("Target", "Estimate", "ScaleReference")]
saveRDS(sd_results, file.path(tempdir(), "standardized-school-results.rds"))
```

For a supported full MML fit with `~Group`, request `scale = "native"` instead;
its fitted residual SD is not substituted for a marginal population SD.
The fixed N(0,1) case uses known SD one. CML estimates no such SD, and this MML
consumer does not extend inference to partial MML fits or GPCM interactions.
Numerical eligibility means that source, information and finer-grid checks
passed. `CoverageQualified = FALSE` and the retained marginal-identification
state keep finite-sample performance and global identification separate from
those checks. These intervals require the declared response/population model
and independent Persons; they are not a calibrated DFF classification.

### Comparing with MH or ordinal logistic DIF

`mantel_haenszel_table()` now supplies a separate binary MH comparison with
explicit matching strata and one response per Person and target. Its default
conditional exact inference uses `stats::mantelhaen.test()`; an asymptotic
option is also available. `analyze_dff()` retains its residual and refit routes.
`ordinal_logistic_table()` supplies the independent-Person cumulative-logit
comparison through the optional `ordinal` package. Pooled repeated-rating
comparisons remain planned work.
First specify what each result describes:

| Procedure | Quantity being compared |
| --- | --- |
| Residual DFF | Group difference in mean observed-minus-expected score; descriptive |
| Linked refit DFF | Group difference in a facet parameter, conditional on baseline anchors |
| Binary Mantel--Haenszel (MH) | A common group odds ratio conditional on declared matching strata |
| Cumulative ordinal logistic | Group and matching-by-group terms in a proportional-odds response model |

First declare the intended response roster and rating plan before running the
methods. Passing that roster through residual `analyze_dff(data = ...)` now
selects the fitted observations by Person, all facets, score, weight and
repeated-response multiplicity. It uses the original fitted expectations,
without recalibrating on the selected subset. The same contract applies to
`dif_interaction_table()`.

Inspect `$cases` in each result: residual output maps `InputRow` in the supplied
data to `FitRow` in `fit$prep$data`; MH/ordinal output identifies input rows
with `Row`. Missing groups, invalid responses and responses absent from the
fit cannot silently acquire another observation's residual. Requesting more
copies than the fit contains is rejected. Identical fitted copies can be
exchanged for this descriptive calculation only when their model moments
agree; their `FitRow` assignment does not recover an occasion identity.

Residual `N` counts response rows, while `NPersons` counts distinct Persons.
For example, 12 Persons with three criteria give 36 rows for a rater, not
36 independent Persons. Descriptive residual summaries can retain those rows;
ordinary MH/ordinal inference cannot treat them as independent target responses.
Earlier saved residual summaries must be recomputed from the saved fit and
source data to obtain this matching audit; a model refit is unnecessary.

Method-specific exclusions can still differ: MH removes uninformative strata,
whereas ordinal models may retain their observations. Report these differences
and the matching rule; do not automatically intersect outcome-dependent
inclusion masks and treat that as a prespecified common cohort. Matching rows
is necessary for understanding a comparison, but does not make the methods'
quantities or null hypotheses identical.

The MH result keeps the MH point estimate separately from the conditional
maximum-likelihood estimate used by exact inference. Its `strata` and `cases`
tables retain group/category counts, opposing effects, missing responses and
strata without overlap. Supply multiple matching columns, such as total and
rating plan, through `strata`; continuous values are not silently binned.
The function rejects duplicate Person-target cells. Pointwise intervals are
not simultaneous across targets; Holm adjustment applies to p-values only.
Exact probability-ordered two-sided p-values need not invert equal-tail
confidence intervals. See `?mantel_haenszel_table` for a runnable example.

The ordinal result fits matching-only (M1), matching plus group (M2), and
matching plus group and their interaction (M3) to identical complete rows.
Its `table` separates uniform (M2/M1), nonuniform (M3/M2) and joint (M3/M1)
likelihood-ratio tests, with Holm adjustment across all three tests and targets.
`DeltaNagelkerkeR2` names the pseudo-R-squared definition explicitly. The
`contrasts` table reports M3's reference/focal upper-tail odds ratios at the
endpoints and midpoint of the overlapping matching ranges; values above one
favor higher reference scores. Fits use all complete responses. An interaction
means this odds ratio changes with matching, so one constant group coefficient
does not summarize the full difference.

The separate `proportional_odds` table tests whether slopes can differ across
category cuts, using a global nonproportional alternative. This diagnostic
has its own multiplicity family and does not select which group tests are run.
For binary responses it is not applicable. `models`, `matching` and `cases`
preserve convergence information, group ranges and row exclusions. Empty
declared categories, absent range overlap and numerical failures remain
unavailable; repeated rows are rejected. See `?ordinal_logistic_table` for a
runnable example and the exact numerical checks. All reported p-values are
asymptotic: convergence or a nonsignificant diagnostic does not establish
adequate small-sample inference or proportional odds.

A bounded known-model check illustrates this limit. With three categories,
balanced groups, a fixed matching grid and total N=40, all 1,000 simulated
data sets had computable group tests. Under no group difference and true
proportional odds, the unadjusted joint test rejected in 65/1,000 cases
(6.5%; 95% Monte Carlo Wilson interval 5.1%--8.2%). The proportional-odds
diagnostic was unavailable in 42 cases and rejected in 114/958 available
cases (11.9%; interval 10.0%--14.1%), at nominal 5%. Treating its numerical
availability as assurance of a valid 5% test would therefore be misleading.
For the default Holm-adjusted family of three group tests, at least one
rejection occurred in 52/1,000 cases (5.2%; interval 4.0%--6.8%). This family
is separate from the proportional-odds diagnostic and does not repair it.
At N=200 and N=1,000 under the same mechanism, joint rejection was 4.7% and
4.6%, and diagnostic rejection was 5.8% and 4.5%, with all results available.
These particular conditions do not establish a universal sample-size rule.
The function offers asymptotic comparisons, not qualified small-sample tests.
No significance cutoff or numerical tolerance was changed in response to
these results; the diagnostic does not determine whether group comparisons are run.

Matching is a substantive choice. In the binary Rasch case with a common
item set and invariant other items, conditioning on the **total including
the studied item** removes the group ability distribution from that item's
conditional response. Removing the studied item can leave group differences
even without IRT DIF ([Holland and Thayer, 1986, pp. 14--18](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2330-8516.1986.tb00186.x)).
This is not a general endorsement of any total score. Contamination by other
DIF items, missing responses and different rater/task plans require separate
attention. In a many-facet assignment, two persons with the same total may
have faced different raters or tasks. Specify common exposure or an explicit
plan adjustment with overlap before treating their totals as comparable.

For each target, retain the persons, group coding, category order, matching
definition, exclusions and rating plan. Repeated ratings from a Person are
not independent new persons in ordinary MH tables or logistic likelihoods.
A comparison must account for that dependence; silently averaging ratings
changes the response being analyzed. Connectedness alone does not resolve
either problem.

MH can miss effects that reverse direction across matching strata.
Rogers and Swaminathan's study also used different purification procedures
for MH and logistic regression, so its comparison is not solely a change of
test statistic ([1993, pp. 111--115](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662169301700201)).
Report uniform and nonuniform terms separately when fitting a logistic
comparison. In Zumbo's three-model sequence, add the group term to the
matching-only model, then add the matching-by-group interaction; the joint
test compares the last model with the first (1999, pp. 23--27).

The cumulative proportional-odds assumption in that ordinal model is
different from the adjacent-category structure of RSM/PCM and is not
generally satisfied by it. Check the matching-response relationship and
model adequacy before interpreting a difference between procedures as DFF.
Pseudo-R-squared definitions and their changes must be named: the historical
`.130` screen in Zumbo's application is not a universal cutoff or a default
for mfrmr. A nonsignificant result is not evidence that differential
functioning is absent, and statistical DIF alone does not establish bias.

Zumbo, B. D. (1999). *A handbook on the theory and methods of differential
item functioning (DIF): Logistic regression modeling as a unitary framework
for binary and Likert-type (ordinal) item scores*. Ottawa, ON: Directorate of
Human Resources Research and Evaluation, Department of National Defense.

### Compare an explicitly shared response roster

The following self-contained example puts the three procedures beside each
other. It requires the optional `ordinal` package. The binary Rasch design has
240 independent Persons answering the same eight items once each. Both groups
have the same item difficulties, but different ability distributions. These
synthetic data illustrate how to assemble and audit a comparison; this one
sample is not a validation study or a recommended sample size.

Here `Total` includes the studied item and is computed only after checking the
complete common item roster. MH conditions on each total separately; the
logistic models instead assume a linear relationship with total on the logit
scale. Even in this Rasch example, those are different matching models.
The residual calculation uses the fitted Person and item parameters.

```{r dff-comparison-input, eval = !is_cran_check && requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
library(mfrmr)
set.seed(241010)
group_order <- c("Reference", "Focal")
person_group <- rep(group_order, each = 120)
ability <- rnorm(240, mean = ifelse(person_group == "Focal", 0.5, -0.5))
shared <- expand.grid(Person = seq_len(240), Item = paste0("I", 1:8),
                      KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
shared$Group <- person_group[shared$Person]
difficulty <- setNames(seq(-1, 1, length.out = 8), paste0("I", 1:8))
shared$Score <- rbinom(nrow(shared), 1,
  plogis(ability[shared$Person] - difficulty[shared$Item]))
stopifnot(!anyNA(shared), all(table(shared$Person, shared$Item) == 1L))
shared$Total <- ave(shared$Score, shared$Person, FUN = sum)

shared_fit <- fit_mfrm(shared, person = "Person", facets = "Item",
                       score = "Score", method = "JML", model = "RSM")
residual <- analyze_dff(shared_fit, facet = "Item", group = "Group",
  data = shared, focal = group_order[2], method = "residual")
mh <- mantel_haenszel_table(shared, person = "Person", target = "Item",
  score = "Score", group = "Group", strata = "Total", groups = group_order)
ologit <- ordinal_logistic_table(shared, person = "Person", target = "Item",
  score = "Score", group = "Group", matching = "Total",
  groups = group_order, categories = 0:1)
```

First retain each method's response audit. The join below uses original row
numbers from the **same** `shared` data, not the position of a row in a result
table. It retains exclusions rather than choosing the intersection of the
methods' retained rows. With one response per Person-item, the counts below
are also distinct-Person counts within each item and group.

```{r dff-comparison-audit, eval = !is_cran_check && requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
case_audit <- rbind(
  data.frame(Method = "Residual", Row = residual$cases$InputRow,
    Included = residual$cases$Included, Reason = residual$cases$Reason),
  data.frame(Method = "MH", mh$cases[c("Row", "Included", "Reason")]),
  data.frame(Method = "Logistic", ologit$cases[c("Row", "Included", "Reason")])
)
case_audit$Target <- shared$Item[case_audit$Row]
case_audit$Person <- shared$Person[case_audit$Row]
case_audit$Group <- shared$Group[case_audit$Row]
case_audit$Count <- 1L
case_counts <- aggregate(Count ~ Target + Method + Group + Included + Reason,
                         data = case_audit, FUN = sum)
case_counts[case_counts$Target == "I2", ]
```

Next align effect direction explicitly. `focal` above makes the residual
contrast Reference minus Focal. All odds ratios below are Reference/Focal
odds of a higher score. Thus a positive residual difference and an odds ratio
above one point in the same score direction, but **their magnitudes cannot be
compared**. The MH column uses the conditional maximum-likelihood estimate
from the default exact analysis; the distinct MH estimator remains in
`mh$table$MHOddsRatio`. Logistic values come from M3 and can change direction
over total scores. Keep their matching values and numerical status visible.

```{r dff-comparison-effects, eval = !is_cran_check && requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
r <- residual$dif_table
stopifnot(all(r$Group1 == group_order[1]), all(r$Group2 == group_order[2]))
effects <- data.frame(Target = r$Level, ResidualDifference = r$Contrast,
  ResidualStatus = ifelse(is.finite(r$Contrast), "descriptive", "unavailable"))
m <- mh$table[c("Target", "OddsRatio", "Status")]
names(m)[2:3] <- c("MH_ExactOR", "MH_Status")
effects <- merge(effects, m, by = "Target", all = TRUE)
mid <- subset(ologit$contrasts, Position == "OverlapMid",
              select = c(Target, Matching, OddsRatio, Status))
names(mid)[2:4] <- c("TotalAtMidpoint", "Logistic_MidOR", "Logistic_Status")
effects <- merge(effects, mid, by = "Target", all = TRUE)
effects[effects$Target == "I2", ]

# Preserve endpoint effects; a midpoint alone can conceal a crossing effect.
subset(ologit$contrasts, Target == "I2")
subset(mh$table, Target == "I2", select = c(Target, NReference, NFocal,
  Lower, Upper, PValue, PAdjusted, Status, IntervalStatus))
subset(ologit$table, Target == "I2", select = c(Target, Comparison,
  DeltaNagelkerkeR2, PValue, PAdjusted, Status))
```

In the displayed sample, residual and logistic calculations use 120 Persons
per group for I2. MH uses 96 Reference and 97 Focal Persons; its audit accounts
for the other 47 responses in constant-response strata. This is a difference
in usable conditional information, not an unnoticed change of the input
roster. At total 0 or 8, the item response is determined by the total itself.
Logistic endpoint odds ratios are predictions from its smooth response model;
they are not empirical odds ratios in those degenerate strata. Overlapping
matching ranges alone do not establish response support or a correct linear
logit relationship. A binary proportional-odds diagnostic cannot check that
relationship.

All eight items were analyzed before displaying I2, chosen in advance as the
example target. MH adjusts across eight item tests; logistic adjusts across
24 item-by-comparison tests. These are separate families, not an adjustment
for selecting among methods. Residual differences have no p-values. MH's
intervals are pointwise; logistic contrasts here have no intervals. For these
binary data the proportional-odds diagnostic is `not_applicable_binary`, not
evidence that proportional odds holds for a future ordinal analysis.

Read the case counts before interpreting different results: MH can omit
constant-response or single-group strata that logistic retains. Logistic
`Included = TRUE` means a row was supplied to a model, not that estimation
succeeded; inspect the effect/test statuses and `ologit$models`. A missing
effect stays `NA`, with its reason, rather than being replaced by zero or
removed from the comparison. The descriptive JML residuals do not acquire
inferential validity from the other methods' p-values.

To retain this analysis, save the input, matching definition, calibration and
complete results together. Later displays can be rebuilt from this object
without rerunning the models.

```{r dff-comparison-save, eval = FALSE}
comparison <- list(data = shared, groups = group_order, categories = 0:1,
